newsitem.title: UK: UK government likely to survive confidence vote.
newsitem.headline: UK government likely to survive confidence vote.

text.p: Britain's opposition Labour party will pursue attempts to bring down the beleaguered government of Prime Minister John Major on Monday, even though it knows its chances of success are minimal.

Major wants to stay in power long enough to call a general election on his preferred date of May 1 but Labour, which has a commanding opinion poll lead, wants to oust the ruling Conservatives as soon as possible.

Labour leader Tony Blair admitted the odds were stacked against him in Monday's vote, which will formally decide whether to censure Agriculture Minister Douglas Hogg for his handling of a protracted crisis over mad cow disease.
The government, if it loses, would have to face a confidence vote the next day. If he lost that vote, Major would have to call an early general election.
"We are confident that we will win the argument. Winning the vote will be more difficult," Blair wrote in the Express on Sunday.
"We will muster as much support as we can, but are aware that for now, at least, the government can probably scrape through."

To win, Labour would need the support of the minority Ulster Unionist Party (UUP), angry over the government's failure to get the European Union to lift a ban on British beef exports imposed due to fears of mad cow disease.
But Labour's hopes were dented when the Ulster Unionists complained that they had not been consulted over the decision to call the vote.
"I think the opposition has got its timing wrong, it's got its objectives wrong and it has got its relationship with other parties wrong," UUP parliamentarian Ken Maginnis told BBC television.
The Times newspaper said Hogg would win UUP support by announcing the first steps towards lifting the beef ban in Northern Ireland, a story denied by the Conservatives.
"We have not bribed or bought off anyone to my knowledge and I have no idea how the Ulster Unionists will vote," Welsh Secretary William Hague told the BBC.
The government is taking no chances. Foreign Secretary Malcolm Rifkind and his deputy Jeremy Hanley are cutting short official overseas visits to get back in time to vote.
The Conservatives have 323 voting members in the lower chamber, a number matched by the combined opposition parties. In the event of a tie, the speaker's casting vote would ensure Major's survival.
Major must call elections by May 22 at the end of the five-year parliamentary term, but constitutionally he has the power to go the polls when he chooses.
